title: Java gives you several ready-made executors — newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newScheduledThreadPool, and ForkJoinPool. When would you pick each one? Why is ForkJoinPool excellent for CPU-heavy recursive work but a poor choice for blocking IO?
shortTitle: Fixed vs Cached vs Scheduled pool?

s1_definition.profdef: The `Executors` factory and the `ForkJoinPool` class give you four common pool shapes. A fixed thread pool holds a constant number of threads and queues extra work, which gives predictable resource use under steady load. A cached thread pool creates new threads on demand and reuses idle ones, which suits short-lived bursty tasks but can grow without bound. A scheduled thread pool runs tasks after a delay or on a repeating schedule. A fork/join pool uses a work-stealing deque per thread and is designed for divide-and-conquer recursive computation; it excels at CPU-bound recursion but behaves badly when its threads block on IO because blocked threads cannot steal or be stolen from.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India staffing different desks. A fixed thread pool is a branch with exactly ten tellers hired for the year — predictable cost, and extra customers wait in line. A cached thread pool is a branch that hires a temp the instant a customer walks in and lets temps go home after a minute idle — great for sudden rushes, dangerous if a thousand customers arrive because you would hire a thousand temps. A scheduled thread pool is the clerk who runs the interest posting job every night at 2 a.m. A fork/join pool is a team that splits a huge counting job — counting all of Rajesh's transactions — into halves, halves of halves, and whoever finishes early grabs work from a busy colleague's pile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fixed for steady bounded load, cached for short bursts, scheduled for timed jobs, and fork/join for CPU recursion but never for blocking IO.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The `Executors` factory and the `ForkJoinPool` class give you four common pool shapes. A fixed thread pool holds a constant number of threads and queues extra work, which gives predictable resource use under steady load. A cached thread pool creates new threads on demand and reuses idle ones, which suits short-lived bursty tasks but can grow without bound. A scheduled thread pool runs tasks after a delay or on a repeating schedule. A fork/join pool uses a work-stealing deque per thread and is designed for divide-and-conquer recursive computation; it excels at CPU-bound recursion but behaves badly when its threads block on IO because blocked threads cannot steal or be stolen from.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India staffing different desks. A fixed thread pool is a branch with exactly ten tellers hired for the year — predictable cost, and extra customers wait in line. A cached thread pool is a branch that hires a temp the instant a customer walks in and lets temps go home after a minute idle — great for sudden rushes, dangerous if a thousand customers arrive because you would hire a thousand temps. A scheduled thread pool is the clerk who runs the interest posting job every night at 2 a.m. A fork/join pool is a team that splits a huge counting job — counting all of Rajesh's transactions — into halves, halves of halves, and whoever finishes early grabs work from a busy colleague's pile.

**One line to remember:** Fixed for steady bounded load, cached for short bursts, scheduled for timed jobs, and fork/join for CPU recursion but never for blocking IO.

sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India needs four different background behaviors and the team keeps reaching for the wrong executor.

Problem 1 — Steady trade settlement. A continuous stream of trades needs processing at a predictable rate, and the operations team wants predictable memory. This is exactly what a fixed thread pool provides: a constant number of workers so memory and CPU are bounded and stable.

Problem 2 — Burst of SMS alerts. When the market opens, thousands of short notification tasks fire for a few seconds then go quiet. A fixed pool would queue them and add latency; what fits is a cached pool that spins up temporary threads for the burst and releases them afterward — but only because these tasks are short.

Problem 3 — Nightly interest posting. Every day at a fixed time the bank posts interest to Rajesh's SAV2001. This is exactly a scheduled pool with a fixed-rate or fixed-delay repeating task.

Problem 4 — Summing a million transaction amounts. The bank must total every amount in a huge in-memory array to reconcile the ledger. This is pure CPU recursion, the ideal case for a fork/join pool using a RecursiveTask and work stealing.

The mini-project builds an `ExecutorChooser` that returns the right executor for a named workload, a `TransactionSumTask` RecursiveTask for the reconciliation, and a demo that exercises all four. The test asserts each chooser returns the expected executor type and that the fork/join sum matches a sequential sum.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four named workloads and a one-million-element array of transaction amounts, each 100 paise.

**Step 1.** The chooser receives STEADY_SETTLEMENT and returns a fixed pool of 16 threads with an unbounded queue. The data is just an ExecutorService reference; a submitted settlement task runs on one of the 16 threads.

**Step 2.** The chooser receives SMS_BURST and returns a cached pool. Five SMS tasks arrive almost at once; the pool creates threads on demand (up to five here) and will reap them after 60 seconds idle.

**Step 3.** The chooser receives NIGHTLY_INTEREST and returns a scheduled pool. The demo schedules the interest task with zero delay so it runs immediately, but in production it would repeat every 24 hours.

**Step 4.** The chooser receives LEDGER_SUM and returns a fork/join pool. The `TransactionSumTask` splits the array in half repeatedly. Each split forks the left half onto the current thread's deque and computes the right half directly.

**Step 5.** Idle fork/join threads steal pending left-half tasks from busy threads' deques, keeping all cores busy. The halves join back up the tree until the root returns the grand total: one million times 100 equals 100,000,000 paise.

```
INFO  STEADY_SETTLEMENT → FixedThreadPool(16) (predictable load)
INFO  Settling trade for SAV2001
INFO  SMS_BURST → CachedThreadPool (short bursty tasks)
INFO  SMS alert #0 to CUR3001
INFO  SMS alert #4 to CUR3001
INFO  NIGHTLY_INTEREST → ScheduledThreadPool(2) (timed job)
INFO  Posting interest to SAV2001
INFO  LEDGER_SUM → ForkJoinPool (CPU recursion, work stealing)
INFO  Ledger total (paise): 100000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: workload name  +  1,000,000 transaction amounts
    │
    ▼
  ExecutorChooser.choose(workload)
    │
    ├─ STEADY_SETTLEMENT ─→ FixedThreadPool(16) ─→ unbounded queue ─→ 16 workers
    │
    ├─ SMS_BURST ─────────→ CachedThreadPool ───→ SynchronousQueue ─→ N temp threads
    │                                               (reaped after 60s idle)
    │
    ├─ NIGHTLY_INTEREST ──→ ScheduledThreadPool(2) ─→ delay queue ─→ timed runs
    │
    └─ LEDGER_SUM ────────→ ForkJoinPool ─→ per-thread deques + work stealing
                                 │
                                 ▼
                    TransactionSumTask.compute()
                       split [0..1,000,000)
                        ├─ fork left [0..500,000)   (pushed to deque)
                        └─ compute right [500,000..1,000,000)
                             ... recurse until chunk ≤ 1000 ...
                        join → sum halves → 100,000,000 paise

  WARNING: if a ForkJoin task did Thread.sleep / DB call here,
  the thread blocks, cannot steal, cores go idle → throughput collapse.
  For blocking IO use FixedThreadPool, NOT ForkJoinPool.
```

     ▼           ▼           ▼               ▼
  Fixed(16)   Cached     Scheduled(2)   ForkJoinPool
  core=16     core=0     delay queue    work-stealing deques

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  TransactionSumTask          │  extends RecursiveTask<Long>
  │  - amounts: long[]           │

  ── Decision Chain ──────────────────────────────────────
  1. Steady, bounded load?       → FixedThreadPool
  2. Short bursty independent?   → CachedThreadPool (short only!)
  3. Timed / repeating job?      → ScheduledThreadPool
  4. CPU-heavy recursion?        → ForkJoinPool
  5. Blocking IO inside task?    → NEVER ForkJoinPool → use Fixed

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java gives you four common executor shapes, and choosing the right one comes down to the shape of the workload. I use a fixed thread pool when the load is steady and bounded, such as a continuous stream of trade settlements, because a constant number of threads gives predictable memory and CPU usage. My one caution there is that the default fixed pool uses an unbounded queue, so in production I usually build a ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded queue and a rejection policy to apply back-pressure.

I use a cached thread pool only for large numbers of short, bursty, independent tasks, like a flood of SMS alerts when the market opens. It creates threads on demand and reaps them after sixty seconds idle, so it handles the spike and then shrinks. The critical caveat is that it has no upper bound on threads, so I never use it for long-running or slow tasks, because a backlog of slow tasks would create an unbounded number of threads and crash the JVM.

I use a scheduled thread pool for timed and repeating work, such as posting daily interest to Rajesh's savings account every night. I pick scheduleWithFixedDelay when runs must never overlap and scheduleAtFixedRate when I want runs anchored to a clock, and I am always mindful that fixed-rate runs can bunch up if a run exceeds its period.

For fork/join I explain both its strength and its trap. It is excellent for CPU-bound divide-and-conquer recursion, like summing a million transaction amounts to reconcile the ledger, because each worker has its own deque and idle workers steal work from busy ones, keeping every core busy with almost no contention. But it is a poor choice for blocking IO, because the pool is sized to roughly one thread per core on the assumption that threads are always running. If a fork/join task blocks on a database or network call, that thread is stuck, it cannot steal or be stolen from, cores go idle, and throughput collapses. So my rule is simple: fork/join and parallel streams for CPU recursion, and a fixed or properly sized thread pool for anything that blocks on IO.

keyPoints: Cached: short-lived bursty tasks, no queue
